Module 1.title: Discrete Random Variables and Distributions (Binomial & Poisson)
Module 1.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Discrete Distributions
  • Binomial Distribution: $P(X = x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x q^{n-x}$. Mean $\mu = n p$, Variance $\sigma^2 = n p q$ ($Var < Mean$).
  • Poisson Distribution: $P(X = x) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^x}{x!}$. Mean $\mu = \lambda$, Variance $\sigma^2 = \lambda$ ($Var = Mean$). Poisson approximation to Binomial occurs when $n \to \infty, p \to 0$ with $n p = \lambda$.
Module 1.detailed_notes:
Module 1 Reference: Probability

Properties of Expectation: $E[aX + b] = a E[X] + b$, $Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X)$. Moment Generating Function: $M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]$.
Module 1.textbook_html:
1.1 Discrete Probability Distributions in Engineering

Random variables represent mathematical mappings from sample spaces to the real number continuum. The Binomial distribution models the number of successes $x$ across $n$ independent Bernoulli trials with constant probability $p$:

$$P(X = x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1 - p)^{n-x}, \quad x = 0, 1, 2, \dots, n$$

Module 2.title: Continuous Random Variables (Uniform and Normal Distributions)
Module 2.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Continuous Distributions
  • Normal (Gaussian) Distribution: $f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$. Standard normal variate $Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim N(0, 1)$.
  • Symmetry: Bell-shaped, symmetric about mean ($Mean = Median = Mode = \mu$). Total area under curve equals $1$. $68.26\%$ within $\mu \pm \sigma$, $95.44\%$ within $\mu \pm 2\sigma$, $99.73\%$ within $\mu \pm 3\sigma$.
Module 2.detailed_notes:
Module 2 Reference: Normal Variates

Uniform Distribution: $f(x) = \frac{1}{b - a}$ for $a \le x \le b$. Mean $\mu = \frac{a+b}{2}$, Variance $\sigma^2 = \frac{(b-a)^2}{12}$.
Module 2.textbook_html:
2.1 The Gaussian Normal Probability Distribution

The Central Limit Theorem establishes that the arithmetic sum of a large number of independent random variables tends toward a Normal distribution, regardless of the underlying distribution of individual variables. This governs quality control tolerances and engineering measurement uncertainties.

Module 3.title: Sampling Theory and Statistical Hypothesis Testing (t-Test and Large Samples)
Module 3.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Hypothesis Testing
  • Null ($H_0$) vs Alternative ($H_1$) Hypothesis: $H_0$ tests no significant difference. Level of significance $\alpha$ (typically $0.05$ or $0.01$).
  • Large Sample Test for Mean ($n \ge 30$): Test statistic $Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}$. Critical value for two-tailed test at $5\%$ is $Z_{0.025} = 1.96$.
  • Small Sample Student's t-Test ($n < 30$): $t = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}$ with degrees of freedom $\nu = n - 1$. Sample variance $s^2 = \frac{\sum (X_i - \bar{X})^2}{n - 1}$.
Module 3.detailed_notes:
Module 3 Reference: Hypothesis Testing

Two-sample t-test for difference of means with pooled variance $S_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}$.
Module 3.textbook_html:
3.1 Principles of Statistical Inference and Hypothesis Testing

Hypothesis testing provides a systematic mathematical decision rule to determine whether observed experimental differences between sample statistics and theoretical population parameters arise from true physical phenomena or purely random sampling fluctuations.

Module 4.title: Complex Functions, Cauchy-Riemann Equations and Harmonic Conjugates
Module 4.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Analytic Functions & C-R Equations
  • Analytic Function (Regular/Holomorphic): A single-valued function $f(z) = u(x,y) + i v(x,y)$ whose complex derivative $f'(z)$ exists at every point in domain $D$.
  • Cauchy-Riemann (C-R) Equations: $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}$$
  • Harmonic Functions: If $f(z) = u + iv$ is analytic, both real part $u$ and imaginary part $v$ satisfy Laplace's equation: $\nabla^2 u = \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0$. $v$ is termed the harmonic conjugate of $u$.
  • Milne-Thomson Method: Constructing analytic $f(z)$ directly from $u(x,y)$: $f'(z) = u_x(z, 0) - i u_y(z, 0)$, then integrate with respect to $z$.
Module 4.detailed_notes:
Module 4 Reference: Complex Functions

Polar form of Cauchy-Riemann equations: $\frac{\partial u}{\partial r} = \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial v}{\partial \theta}$, $\frac{\partial v}{\partial r} = -\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial u}{\partial \theta}$.
Module 4.textbook_html:
4.1 Complex Differentiation and the Cauchy-Riemann Equations

Let $f(z) = u(x,y) + i v(x,y)$ be a complex function of $z = x + iy$. The derivative is defined by the limit:

$$f'(z) = \lim_{\Delta z \to 0} \frac{f(z + \Delta z) - f(z)}{\Delta z}$$

For this limit to be unique, it must evaluate to the identical value regardless of the trajectory along which $\Delta z = \Delta x + i \Delta y o 0$ in the complex plane. Approaching along the real axis ($\Delta y = 0$) and imaginary axis ($\Delta x = 0$) yields the necessary Cauchy-Riemann equations:

$$u_x = v_y \quad \text{and} \quad u_y = -v_x$$

Module 5.title: Complex Integration, Cauchy's Integral Formula and Residue Theorem
Module 5.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Complex Integration & Residues
  • Cauchy's Integral Theorem: If $f(z)$ is analytic within and on simple closed contour $C$: $\oint_C f(z) dz = 0$.
  • Cauchy's Integral Formula: If $z_0$ is inside closed contour $C$: $\oint_C \frac{f(z)}{z - z_0} dz = 2\pi i f(z_0)$. For $n$-th derivative: $\oint_C \frac{f(z)}{(z - z_0)^{n+1}} dz = \frac{2\pi i}{n!} f^{(n)}(z_0)$.
  • Residue at Simple Pole: $\text{Res}(f, z_0) = \lim_{z \to z_0} (z - z_0) f(z) = \frac{P(z_0)}{Q'(z_0)}$.
  • Cauchy's Residue Theorem: $\oint_C f(z) dz = 2\pi i \sum_{k=1}^m \text{Res}(f, z_k)$ (sum of residues at all isolated singularities inside $C$).
Module 5.detailed_notes:
Module 5 Reference: Complex Integration

Taylor series expansion is valid in disk $|z-z_0| < R$. Laurent series $f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n (z-z_0)^n + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{b_n}{(z-z_0)^n}$ is valid in annulus $r < |z-z_0| < R$. The coefficient $b_1$ is the Residue.
Module 5.textbook_html:
5.1 Cauchy's Integral Theorem and Residue Evaluation

Complex line integrals possess extraordinary analytical power. If an integrand $f(z)$ is analytic inside a simply connected domain bounded by closed contour $C$, Green's theorem demonstrates that the line integral vanishes completely: $\oint_C f(z) dz = 0$. When isolated poles exist inside $C$, the integral is evaluated via Cauchy's Residue Theorem:

$$\oint_C f(z) dz = 2\pi i \sum_{k=1}^m \text{Res}(f, z_k)$$
